en: Oṃ, homage to Gaṇeśa!
Having prostrated before Govinda, who is unborn, imperishable, and the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
In the *Smṛtitattva*, the illustrious Raghunandana expounds the *Divyatattva* (the principles of ordeal).
Then, in that regard, Bṛhaspati [enumerated] the divine ordeals:
the balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation (kośa).
The sixth is declared to be *taṇḍula*, and the seventh is *taptamāṣaka*.
The eighth is called *phāla*, and the ninth is remembered as *dharmaja*.
All these divine ordeals were prescribed by the Self-Existent One himself.

Now, what is that "divine" (divya)? It is well known in the world that the divine is that which determines even that which cannot be determined by human means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By the word "even" (*api*), it is indicated that this [divine proof] applies even in cases where human means of knowledge such as documents, witnesses, and possession exist, yet the acceptance of the balance (*ghaṭa*) and other [ordeals] is required. Therefore, the divine is a means of knowledge distinct from the threefold human means of knowledge characterized as documents, witnesses, and possession. Furthermore, that which is divine does not have existence alone as its object; rather, it perceives both existence and non-existence without distinction. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the divine proofs for cases of grave accusation (*mahābhiyoga*): [p.80] *In cases of grave accusation, the following divine proofs are declared: the balance, fire, water, poison, and holy water.* || 2.95 ||* *The balance is for those weighing one hundred *paṇas*; fire for those weighing two hundred; water for those weighing three hundred; and poison and holy water for those weighing four hundred.* || 2.96 ||* *In cases of grave accusation, these five are prescribed; in cases of minor accusation, however, the ordeal of truth is ordained.* || 2.97 ||* *In a dispute concerning a debt, the defendant may choose whichever [proof] he prefers; in all other matters, the plaintiff shall choose.* || 2.98 ||* *In cases involving women, minors, the blind, the aged, the sick, the lame, and those accused of minor offenses, the ordeal of truth is ordained.* || 2.99 ||* *For those who have committed a crime, for those who have been previously defeated in court, and for those who are suspicious, the ordeal of fire or water is ordained.* || 2.100 ||* *In disputes regarding land, the ordeal of poison or holy water is prescribed; Fire, water, poison, and the balance are the ordeals here for the sake of purification, in cases of serious accusations, when the accuser is liable for the penalty.

[Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.95] "For the sake of purification" means for the removal of doubt regarding a contested matter. "In cases of serious accusations" refers to accusations of the most grave nature, such as the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). "When the accuser is liable for the penalty": *śīrṣaka* means the principal head, namely the fourth part of the legal proceeding characterized by victory or defeat; by this, punishment is indicated. One who "stands upon that" (*śīrṣakastha*) is one who is subject to the punishment incurred therein; this is the meaning.
The *Kālikāpurāṇa* clarifies the great charges:

"In cases of accusations regarding another's wife, theft, and approaching those who should not be approached, as well as in cases of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) and royal crimes, the ordeal shall be administered. (Dhko 470)
When a disagreement or a dispute has arisen and a wager has been established,
the lord of the earth shall administer the ordeal there, beginning with that of the head.
Likewise in the case of an accusation of adultery with another's wife, or where there are many litigants.
The divine [image] should be headless for the sake of the purification of the self; thus says Pitāmaha.

One should avoid divine ordeals that are devoid of a "head" (śiras). However, the four ordeals beginning with the *dhaṭa* (balance), as well as the *kośa* (oath), are traditionally held to be "headless. Smṛti states that the *kośa* may be employed in cases other than those involving a major charge (*mahābhiyoga*). One should cause the *kośa* to be administered even in minor matters. Since Yājñavalkya declares that the accuser (*abhiyoktṛ*)—the litigant—is subject to the "head," it is established that the burden of the charge (*abhiyoga*) rests upon the one who undergoes the divine ordeal.
Kātyāyana has stated clearly:
"No one should subject the plaintiff to ordeals;
those expert in ordeals should administer the ordeal to the defendant. [K 411]
Yājñavalkya states that the defendant may accept the ordeal on behalf of the plaintiff as well:
"Either party may undergo [the ordeal] by mutual consent, while the other must provide the head-fee (*śiras*);
or one may undergo it even without the head-fee in cases of treason against the king or mortal sins. (YDh 2.96)
The other, being prosecuted, shall undergo corporal punishment or pay a monetary fine;
thus says Bṛhaspati.
Witnesses may fall into disagreement due to affection, anger, or greed; however, no disagreement ever arises regarding a divine ordeal performed according to the prescribed rule.
(11) [B 8.14] "Disagreement" means a deviation from the truth.
As for the statement of Kātyāyana:
"Divine means of proof are not prescribed when witnesses are available;
nor, in legal disputes where a written document exists, should there be either divine ordeals or witnesses. (K 233)
Thus, this applies when there is a witness endowed with such qualities.
As Vyāsa says:
"That which is administered by the power of gems, mantras, or herbs, or given without following the prescribed ritual..."
A witness endowed with good qualities should not give false testimony, even regarding a divine ordeal.
(13) [Vyā 110] For this very reason, Nārada says: "Even when other means of proof have failed, one should constrain him by means of an oath. (14) [N 1.239ab]
"Ardayet" means he should afflict or cause pain; that is to say, he should compel [the witness]. Nārada states the oaths as follows:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, and gold;
deities, the feet of the ancestors, gifts bestowed, and meritorious deeds. (15) [N 1.248]
In all legal disputes, one may touch the hair of one's sons, wives, or friends,
or even drink from the royal water-vessel as an ordeal. [Dhko 441]
Thus these oaths have been declared by Manu for minor causes. Bṛhaspati says:
The ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rule by those expert in ordeals.
But that which is offered contrary to what was prescribed is not capable of accomplishing the goal to be achieved.
(17) [B 8.15] Offerings given at an improper place or time, or those performed outside by adversaries, always produce deviation; of this there is no doubt in this world. (18) [B 8.16]

"Those performed by outsiders" means those conducted without an accuser; this, however, is the general rule. For those intent on self-purification, there is the provision of ordeals even without an accuser. And so says Nārada:
"In the case of those suspected by kings, or those pointed out by bandits..."
And for those intent on the purification of the self, the divine ordeal may be administered, except for the head.
Now, Kātyāyana describes the location for the divine ordeal:

One should employ [the ritual] at the gate of the king for those men who have been accused in the place of Indra, who are great sinners, and who have engaged in treason against the sovereign. (20) [K 434] [p.84]
For those born of inverse unions, a divine ordeal should be administered for cases involving quadrupeds;
for other matters, the wise declare that it should be conducted in the midst of the assembly hall.
(21) [K 435] "In the place of Indra" means in the place of the banner of Indra.
Now, regarding the divine periods of time,
the Grandfather [Brahmā] said:
"Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha."
These months are common to all and are not in conflict with the celestial seasons. The balance (dhaṭa) is declared suitable for all seasons, but one should avoid it when the wind blows.
Fire is proclaimed [as appropriate] during the cool season, winter, and the rainy season.
"In autumn and summer, water [is used]; in winter and early spring, poison;
but the ordeal by balance may always be administered.
Thus says the Mitākṣarā. (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 2.97)
Nārada said:
O King, there should be no purification by water during the cold season, nor purification by fire during the heat of summer;
one should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor employ the balance scale in a strong wind.

In cold weather, during the *hemanta* and *śiśira* seasons and the rains; in hot weather, during the *grīṣma* and *śarad* seasons. Regarding the prohibition of poison during the rains, it refers specifically to the prohibition of poison exceeding four *yava*s in measure, based on the forthcoming statement of Nārada: "In the rainy season, [the dose shall be] only four *yava*s. As for rice and the other substances, since no specific time is mentioned, they may be used at all times. Since poison is specifically prohibited during the rains here, one should perform other ordeals even during the rains—provided they are not in the month of Siṃha—as the forthcoming text prohibits the mere performance of the ordeal during the month of Siṃha. Therefore...
"One should avoid all ritual acts while the sun is on its southern course and while Hari is asleep"—this [rule] does not apply here. According to *Jyotiṣa*:
"When Jupiter is situated in Leo or Capricorn, and likewise when he has set..."

One desiring victory should not conduct an examination during an intercalary month (malamāsa). Furthermore, when the sun is pure, when Jupiter is present, and when Venus has not set, nor when the sun is situated in Leo— during these times, an examination is not commended by the wise.
Neither on the eighth nor on the fourteenth day should there be an examination for penance;
likewise, neither an examination nor a marriage should take place on a Saturday or a Tuesday.

In the phrase "when the Sun is purified and Jupiter [is likewise]," the word "is recommended" (*śasyate*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus it is stated in the *Dīpakalikā*: "One should not perform the ordeal when Venus is in its setting, nor when the Sun is in the eighth house, nor when the Sun is with Jupiter, nor in the month of birth, nor when the Moon is in the eighth house, nor during the *Viṣṭi* yoga, nor in a month called *mala*, nor on a Tuesday or Saturday, nor under the stars of one's birth. Furthermore, the examination should be conducted in the morning when the *nāḍī-nakṣatra* is absent, when Jupiter and the Moon (the Lord of Night) are purified by their respective stars, at an auspicious ascendant where the rising sign is a movable, dual, or fixed sign. The Grandfather (*Pitāmaha*) says:
"The King, or his appointed official, should cause the ordeal to be administered in person."
And likewise for learned Brāhmaṇas and for the subjects.
(30) [Pi 51] The meaning is that he should cause the divine ordeal to be administered in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas and the subjects. "Subjects" refers to the ministers and others.
[The constituents of the state are: the sovereign, the minister, the ally, the treasury, the realm, the fort, and the army.
"The constituent elements of the kingdom are the subjects and also the guilds of the citizens," as stated by Amarasiṃha [Amarakośa 2.8.18]. Now, those entitled to the specific divine ordeals:
In this regard, Nārada says:
"The balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya;
water should be administered to a Vaiśya, and poison alone to a Śūdra. (NSm 1.334cd–335ab)
The treasury of all [ordeals] has been declared by the wise to be common;
however, with the exception of poison, the balance is prescribed for all, including Brāhmaṇas. (Dhko 453)

Furthermore, if righteousness were indeed his concern, the ordeal would not be administered to those who have taken vows, those who are severely afflicted, those who are diseased, ascetics, or women. (34) [N 1.256]

Thus, Śūlapāṇi maintains that the divine ordeal (*divya*) is prohibited for women and others, but only with respect to matters other than rice-germ tests (*taṇḍula*). In the *Mitākṣarā*, however, it is stated that in a dispute between a man and a woman, "there is no divine ordeal for women"; rather, this is intended to prohibit an option where either party might proceed by choice (*rucyā*). This is what is meant: in cases of charges involving physical violence (*avaṣṭambha*), if women and others are the accusers, the ordeal belongs only to those being accused; even if these [women] are the ones being accused, the ordeal belongs only to the accusers. But in a mutual accusation, there is indeed an option. Even in that case, it is restricted to the balance (*tulā*) alone. Likewise, in a charge involving suspicion of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth, the ordeal for women and others is the balance alone.
As Yājñavalkya says:
"The balance [is used] for women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick."

For a Śūdra, fire or water is prescribed; for one subject to the ordeal of poison, seven barley grains. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.98) The term "mere woman" (*strīmātra*) refers to women regardless of caste, age, or specific condition, with due regard for their status. A child is one up to sixteen years of age, with due regard for caste distinctions; an elder is one who has mastered the Vedas. This statement is meaningful as a restrictive rule regarding women and others in the general provisions for all ordeals during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Caitra, and Vaiśākha. It does not mean that for women the balance alone is to be used at all times. For it is said: "Poison is not declared for women, nor is water prescribed for them."
"Another should examine their true state by means of the *dhaṭa*, the *kośa*, and so forth" (Dhko 452).

Thus, because purification is prescribed by means of the *dhaṭa*, the *kośa*, and other methods distinct from poison and water, this should be applied accordingly even in the case of children and others. Likewise, for Brahmins and the other castes as well, there is no rule mandating the balance scale (*tulā*) and such at all times;
for purification by means of the *kośa* is ordained for all social classes (*varṇa*).
All these [acts] are for all [castes], except for the Brāhmaṇa, who is exempt from poison.

Thus, because of the recollection of Pitāmaha (Yājñavalkya), this statement is intended solely as a restrictive rule for the balance (*tulā*) and other ordeals when they coincide with the common [seasonal] time. However, at other times, all [ordeals] are prescribed according to their respective seasons. For instance, during the rainy season, fire alone is [prescribed] for everyone. During the two seasons of *hemanta* and *śiśira*, however, there is an option between fire and poison for the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya. But for the Brāhmaṇa, fire alone is used; poison is never [used] for a Brāhmaṇa, due to the prohibition: "Poison is not for a Brāhmaṇa. During the summer and autumn, however, water alone is used. Furthermore, for those such as lepers (*kuṣṭhin*), there is a specific prohibition against fire and the other ordeals.

One should avoid fire for those suffering from skin diseases, water for those with asthma and cough, and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with disorders of bile and phlegm. (38) [Pi 42]

Because of this statement, even at times such as those [specified for] fire and the rest, the ordeal of the balance (*tulā*) and so forth alone becomes the common ordeal for them. Likewise, because of the Smṛti rule—"Water, fire, and poison should be administered to strong men"—and because poison is prohibited in every way for the weak, the ordeals based on specific distinctions of caste, age, and physical condition must be administered by transgressing the stated times. In this regard, it should be understood that for each person, there are primary, secondary, and tertiary ordeals—those specifically excluded, those generally prescribed, and those other than these. For example, the balance (*dhaṭa*) is the primary ordeal for a Brāhmaṇa, while the oath (*koṣa*) is the secondary; water and fire are the tertiary ordeals. This status of being primary, secondary, and tertiary follows from the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the previously cited statement of Nārada; it does not, however, imply that they are ranked as "most excellent" and so forth. Thus, it should be understood from what was stated previously that in other cases as well, an ordeal administered contrary to the rules is incapable of proving the matter to be adjudicated.
Smṛti:
For those who are accused on the basis of physical resistance, one should prescribe ordeals such as the balance and so forth;
and rice and the ordeal of the sacred libation (kośa) should be used in cases of suspicion alone—of this there is no doubt. (39) [Pi 36]
"Here, 'avaṣṭambha' means certainty; some say it refers to being placed upon the head"—thus says the *Vyavahāradīpikā*.
Kātyāyana states: "In the case of untouchables, low-caste slaves, Mlecchas, and evildoers..."
For those born of inverse unions, there is no certainty regarding the king;
therefore, one should prescribe the well-known divine ordeals for them at the appropriate time.
Those are well-known cases, such as the snake and the jar. Likewise:
"But when there is no conflict regarding place or time, one should determine the ordeal as appropriate;
in cases of conflict or the reverse, one should have another person undergo the ordeal. (41) [K 436]

"By another" means through a representative; "should cause to be administered" means he should have it performed. This is in the case where the accused is incapable [of performing the ordeal himself]. For this very reason, the same author states that for those who have committed mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*) and others, the ordeal must be conducted by means of another:
"For those who have killed their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, a child, a woman, or a king;
for those guilty of mortal sins, and especially for atheists... (K 427)
Having spoken thus,
a king devoted to dharma should never administer a divine ordeal; rather,
a divine ordeal is fit for virtuous men who have been accused by these very [means].
Kātyāyana says: One should not employ fire for blacksmiths, nor water for those who live by lotuses; one should not employ rice for a Brāhmaṇa suffering from diseases of the mouth. (44) [K 424abef]

Fire-treatment is not prescribed for those afflicted with leprosy, blindness, deformed nails, and the like; nor is immersion in water prescribed for women or children by those learned in the Dharmaśāstras. (45) [N 1.255cd–313ab]
One should not cause those who are lacking in vigor, emaciated by disease, or afflicted to drown in water;
nor should one cause them to be eliminated by fire, nor purify them by means of poison.
As for that which...

"In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals," so says Pitāmaha (verse 47). This prohibits ordeals when there exist written documents, neighbors, and other such evidence. Even though it is said:
"In a legal proceeding involving violence where no document exists, one should prescribe an ordeal" (verse 48).

Thus says the Smṛti. In other types of disputes, there is no regard for ordeals (*divya*) when documents and the like exist. Nevertheless, in disputes such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), even if witnesses have been presented, if the defendant accepts an ordeal by undertaking its penalty, then an ordeal may indeed take place. This is because witnesses are subject to the possibility of error, whereas an ordeal is faultless; furthermore, it pertains to the true nature of things (*vastutattva*), and Dharma is characterized by that very nature. As Nārada says:
"In that case, Dharma is established in truth, but legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) rests upon witnesses. (NMā 1.11ab)

In a matter that is to be settled by fate (*daiva-sādhya*), one should not employ human effort (*pauruṣa*) through written evidence. (59) [YMtā 2.96, K 224cd] Regarding disputes over immovable property (*sthāvara-vivāda*), when the defendant has accepted a fine and resorted to an ordeal (*divya*), even though there exist visible means of proof such as witnesses from neighboring villages (*sāmanta*), the rule that "the ordeal must be accepted" serves to reject the optionality [of the ordeal]. This statement by Pitāmaha beginning with "in cases of immovable property" (*sthāvareṣu*) is not for the purpose of an absolute prohibition of ordeals; for if there were no written documents or other evidence, a legal decision regarding immovable property and the like would simply not arise. Now, the specific types of ordeals according to the value of the object:

Viṣṇu: "Now, regarding the administration of ordeals (*samayakriyā*): in cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [the ordeal] may be administered at will; in cases of deposits, debts, and theft, it depends on the value of the object. (Vi 9.1–3). The term *samaya* refers to an ordeal. In cases such as treason against the king, the ordeal is administered "at will," meaning in accordance with the king's desire. However, in cases such as deposits and the like, the meaning is that it depends on the gradation of the monetary value of the object.
Bṛhaspati says:
"The number [of kalpas] was declared by Manu to be rooted in the rays of light and the atoms."
In a divine ordeal, that fine shall be applied up to the amount of one kārṣāpaṇa; likewise in matters of discipline.

Poison is to be used when a thousand [kārṣāpaṇas] have been stolen, and fire when three-quarters of a thousand have been taken; water is to be administered when three parts of a thousand remain, and the balance is always to be given for half [of a thousand].
In a case involving a debt of four hundred, the ordeal of the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka) must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains (taṇḍula) are to be given, and for half of that amount, the ordeal of the sacred water-vessel (kośa).
When one hundred has been stolen or denied, the purification by means of Dharma (dharmaśodhana) must be administered.
The members of the court must diligently award a ploughshare to a cow-thief.

This number is prescribed for those of low status; for those of middle status, it is recorded as double that amount, and for those of superior status, it should be determined by the judges as four times that amount.

The particle of light-dust (*raśmirajas*): That minute dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the first of measurements, the triad-atom (*tryasareṇu*). (58) [M 8.132]

Thus it was stated by Manu. Since *kārṣāpaṇa* and *paṇa* are seen as synonyms—given that they are used interchangeably as "a *kārṣāpaṇa*" and "a *paṇa*"—the term *paṇa* should be understood in the context of punishment (*daṇḍe*) in the Vinaya, as well as in expressions such as "a thousand" (*sahasra*). And thus: "One should not administer fire, nor a scale, nor poison for less than a thousand [paṇas]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.99ab). This statement of Yājñavalkya is not contradictory, as it is consistent with the statement of Bṛhaspati when both are understood to refer to cases involving middling and superior offenses. Furthermore, the qualities of birth, action, and virtue are inferior among those who are lowly. And so it is said: [95] "One should not administer fire, nor a scale, nor poison for less than a thousand [paṇas]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.99ab).
This statement of Yājñavalkya is not contradictory, as it is consistent with the statement of Bṛhaspati when both are understood to refer to cases involving middling and superior offenses.
"One should administer the *dhaṭa* ordeal for a fine of one thousand; likewise, the iron ball for half of a thousand;
for half of that, water; and for half of that, poison is prescribed. (Dhko 463).
This statement refers to cases where there is a minor offense, yet it results in loss of caste (*pātitya*). All of this pertains to the subject matter of theft and violent crimes (*sāhasa*).
But regarding denial, Kātyāyana says:
"In a case where there is a denial of what was given, one should cause proof to be established;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value. (K 416)
Having ascertained the measure of all the materials, one should fashion the gold;
having determined the quantity of gold, one should then fashion the divine [image].
Having ascertained the number of gold pieces, it is traditionally taught that poison [is to be administered] in the event of the loss of a hundred.
Upon the destruction of eighty, one should indeed offer fire;
upon the destruction of sixty, water should be given, and at forty, the balance.
If twenty or ten coins are lost, drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, if more than five are lost, then rice grains are used;
for losses of half that amount again, one should touch the heads of one's sons and others.
Therefore, when prosperity and decline occur, worldly activities are prescribed;
by reflecting in this way, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha.
[K 421] Of those made of fine gold.

"Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*" (MDh 8.134cd). Thus, regarding gold measured by eighty *raktikas*, the meaning is that if there is loss or denial of ten, five, or twenty *suvarṇas*, the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (*koṣapāna*) shall be administered. Furthermore, rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are used only when there is suspicion of minor theft, and not in cases of violence (*sāhasa*) and the like.
The settled rule is: "Rice grains are to be administered in cases of theft, and nowhere else. (Pi 163cd)
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Pitāmaha:
"The ordeal of the heated gold ball (*taptamāṣa*) is for suspicion of great theft.
For those accused of great theft, the heated gold ball is ordained. (69) [Dhko 463]
Thus it is stated in the *Vyavahāramātṛkā*. [p.97]
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should purify even that case by means of ordeals.
In disputes where the penalty is the loss of life, if witnesses are available and the litigant resorts to an ordeal, one should not question the witnesses in that instance. (70) [VyMā 316, K 232]
Now follows the procedure for the production of the balance, as taught by Pitāmaha:
having cut down a sacrificial tree in the manner of a sacrificial post (yūpa), preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Having prostrated before the guardians of the world (lokapālas), the wise should prepare the balance.

[Pi 84] The phrase "like a sacrificial post" (yūpavat) indicates an extension (atideśa) of all the procedural requirements prescribed for the cutting of a sacrificial post. And that [procedure] consists of specific elements such as the cutting mantra: "O axe, do not harm him," according to the *Vyavahārapradīpa*. Furthermore:
"The mantra addressed to Soma (saumya) is to be recited when cutting a tree belonging to the forest deities (vānaspatya). [Pi 85]
The balance-beam should be made quadrangular, firm, and likewise straight;
and rings should be provided meaningfully at three places.
(73) [Pi 86] "Rings" refers to circular bands.

The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, and its two feet above it should be equal to that. (74) [Pi 87ab] Here, the "cubit" (*hasta*) mentioned in the *Śāradātilaka* should be understood as the standard measure. As follows:
Those who know the tantras understand a *hasta* to consist of twenty-four *aṅgulas*.
The *mānāṅgula* (measurement-finger) is declared to be fashioned from eight *yavas*—that is, eight grains of barley. [Śati 2.51cd and 2.53ab] (*Yavānām* means of barley-grains.)
"One finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) shall consist of eight grains of barley (*yava*) joined together without being elongated;
a cubit (*hasta*) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths.

Thus it is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*. The measurement, however, is by the side, because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "Six barley-grains are the measure of the side. Regarding the arrangement of the other two [dimensions], the *Kāpila-pañcarātra* says:
O best of sages, with those eight [yavas] it becomes the largest (jyeṣṭha) finger-breadth; with seven barley-corns, the middle (madhyama); and with six, the smallest (kanyasa) is specified.

[The term] *kanayasa* means *kaniṣṭha*. "The two pillars" refers to the feet. "Above the clay" means that they are equal to that, i.e., four cubits (*caturhasta*) high. In reality, however, "above, equal to that" means those two feet which have another piece of wood (*kāṣṭhāntara*) above them, equal to that [clay].
Vyāsa states the measurement of the pillars:
"For two *muṇḍaka* pillars, it is said that two cubits should be buried;
their height, by measure, is stated to be six cubits. (Vyā 118abcd)

[On the two pillars at the front and back: "The two pillars shall be six cubits [in height], equal to [the depth] of two buried cubits; that is to say, four cubits above the ground. However, the distance between them shall be two cubits, or indeed one and a half. (79) [Pi 87cd]

The distance between those two pillars is two cubits, meaning the middle measurement; "one and a half" means two and a half cubits. However, this refers to the case of the five-cubit-long balance mentioned by Viṣṇu: "A balance made from śāla wood should be five cubits long" (Vi 10.3). The *Vyavahāradīpikā* also states the same.
Now follows the procedure for the ordeal by balance, as taught by Pitāmaha:
two cubits [in depth] must be dug for both feet. (81) [Pi 88ab]
In this case, two cubits should be within the earth and four cubits above the earth;
likewise,
the archways (toraṇa) should be constructed in the same manner on both sides.

The two [posts] should always be ten finger-breadths higher than the balance-beam (dhaṭa). [Pi 89] Two downward-facing supports (avalamba) should be made from clay and attached by strings, touching the top of the balance-beam from the two arches (toraṇa). [Pi 90ab–cd]
The ordeal by balance should be performed facing east in a clean place; thus says Nārada. [Pi 91ab] [p.100]
Having secured two sturdy slings upon the two hooks of the balance, one should place a man on one sling and a stone on the other. —
Pitāmaha.
One should arrange darbha grass facing east on both sides of the two scales;
one should weigh the makers in the western scale and auspicious earth in the other.
One should fill that [scale] with bricks, stones, and fine dust. [86] [Dhko 482]

Examiners skilled in weights and measures should be appointed—merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise bell-metal workers. (87) [Pi 94] The balance must always be made by the examiners so that it is perfectly level when suspended. (88) [Pi 95]
And water should be poured by the wise upon the balance;
that balance upon which the water does not float is to be known as even.
Having first weighed the man, one should then lower him [from the scale].
One should always have a sacrificial pit (dhaṭa) constructed, adorned with banners and flags. Then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deities according to this rite,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Facing east and with palms joined in reverence, the *prāḍvivāka* shall then speak.
Regarding the designation *prāḍvivāka*: he is called *prāṭ* because he asks (*pṛcchati*), and *vivāka* because he discerns (*vivecayati*) the matter; such is the *vyavahāramātṛkā*.
And so says Bṛhaspati:
In a dispute, he asks the question and likewise receives the answer;
because he speaks first with kindness, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*. (93) [B 1.69]
Kātyāyana states the etymology of the term *prāḍvivāka*:

"The traditional law (smṛti) says that he asks (*pṛcchati*) the question concerning the legal dispute (*vyavahāra*), thus he is called *prāṭ*; and because he discriminates (*vivecayati*) [the truth], he is therefore known as *prāḍvivāka*. [K 69]

One who asks about the charge (*abhiśāpa*) is the *prāṭ* (questioner); one who subsequently discriminates the appropriate divine ordeal (*divya*) is the *vivāka* (discriminator). Thus, he is the *prāḍvivāka* (the questioner-discriminator). Consequently, the *prāḍvivāka* should first inquire about the case and then deliberate upon what has been presented.
Regarding this rite as being optional (*kāmya*), the *Matsyapurāṇa* prescribes the worship of the nine planets:
"Having performed the sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagrahamakha*), one should then commence the ritual action" (MP 92.138cd).
Otherwise, no desired rite performed by men ever yields its fruit.
Therefore, having weighed and lowered the consecrated image, one should perform the invocation of the Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and the subsequent rites.
The Grandfather said: "Come, come, O Blessed Dharma! Enter into this divine [image], together with the world-protectors and the hosts of Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts."
Having invoked Dharma into the balance, one should subsequently assign the limbs [of the deity].
The limbs refer to the attendant deities and so forth.
Having first established Indra in the east, one should likewise establish Yama (the Lord of the Dead) in the south.
One should place Varuṇa in the western part and Kubera likewise in the north.
One should also install the world-protectors, beginning with Agni, in the corner regions.
Indra is yellow, Yama is dark, and Varuṇa has the luster of crystal.

Kubera, however, has the luster of gold, and Vahni likewise has the luster of gold; Nirṛti is dark-colored, and Vāyu is praised as being smoke-colored. Īśāna should be white, and Ananta is indeed white as well.
Brahmā himself shall be red; thus one should meditate on these in sequence. [Dhko 466] [p.103] A wise man should invoke the Vasus on the right side of Indra. [Pi 62cd]
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, and Anala, || 101 || Pratyuṣas and Prabhāsa—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. [Pi 63cd] Between Deveśa and Īśāna is likewise the path of the Ādityas. [Pi 64ab]
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and likewise Aṃśu and Bhaga;
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
then Aṣṭā, then Viṣṇu, the youngest, born after all others.
"Ajadhanya" and "Jaghanyaja" are epithets of Viṣṇu.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by Manu.
They know that the abode of the Rudras is to the western part of Agni. (104) [Pi 66]
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Girīśa;
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the unconquered Aparājita;
Bhuvanādhiśvara, Kapālī, and Viśāmpati. || 105 || [Pi 67]
Sthāṇu, Bhava, and the Lord Rudra are remembered as the eleven;
"of great fame," "lord of the people," and "the Blessed One" are the qualifying epithets.
One should arrange the station of the Mothers between the Lord of the Pretas and the Rakṣasa:
Brāhmī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā, together with her attendants. 107. [Pi 69ab–70ab]
The term "joined with the Gaṇas" is a qualifying attribute.
They know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti;
the station of the Maruts is said to be in the northern part of Varuṇa. (Pi 70cd–71ab)
Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila,
Māruta, Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, and Jīva— these eight Maruts are proclaimed.
A wise man should invoke Durgā on the northern side of the balance.
And they know that for the worship of these deities by their own names, one should recite them preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with a salutation (*namaskāra*).
The *Brahmapurāṇa* states this specific rule:
"Accompanied by the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and proclaimed with a salutation at the end."
One's own name is designated as the "mantra" of all sentient beings. || 111 ||
By this very procedure, one should offer scents and flowers;
one should perform [this] for each [deity] in the sequence as prescribed.

Because of the designation "mantra" and because of the hearing of the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "by this alone," one should employ the formula: "This substance, Om, obeisance to [Name]. However, the statement in the *Mitākṣarā*, "I offer the *arghya* to Dharma, obeisance," is not authoritative due to a lack of evidence and because it lacks syntactic connection. Pitāmaha says:
"Having given ornaments ending with clothing to Dharma, one should then present the *arghya* and so forth in sequence. (Pi 73cd)
Thereafter, one should provide the offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with ornaments for the limbs;
then one should perform the service beginning with *gandha* and ending with food (*naivedya*).
[Pi 74] The presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) shall perform all of this, as follows:
Then the judge shall be a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
endowed with scriptural learning and observance of vows, tranquil in mind, free from envy,
true to his word, pure, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings. (Dhko 475)
Having fasted, wearing clean garments, and having performed the cleansing of the teeth and so forth,
one should perform the worship of all the deities according to the prescribed rule.
Nārada has declared that red perfumes and flowers [are to be used].
One should first worship the balance with red perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth; thereafter, one should honor the remaining [deities]. (116) [Dhko 475]
The *dharma* is the *dhaṭa*. Likewise, Viṣṇu and Nārada state: "A synonym for *dharma* is designated as *dhaṭa*. (Vi 10.10, N 1.277).

Regarding the remaining [deities], Indra and the others, because there is no distinction, the connection with red [garments] applies everywhere. However, in the *Mitākṣarā*, the restriction to red [garments] applies only to the worship of Dharma. Likewise...
Then, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four directions by those who have mastered the Vedas,
using clarified butter, sacrificial oblation, and fuel-sticks as the means for the sacrifice.
One should offer the oblation with the Sāvitrī mantra, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "svāhā."

Having recited the Gāyatrī preceded by the *praṇava*, and having again recited the *praṇava* ending with the word *svāhā*, one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) one hundred and eight times for each; such is the *Mitākṣarā*. In reality, however, regarding the Gāyatrī-homa, Yogiyājñavalkya states:
"In the rite of homa, [the offering is made] with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, ending with *svāhā*. (BYV 4.40cd) [p.107]

Having recited the *praṇava* and so forth, along with the *gāyatrī* verse accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*, and having again recited the *praṇava* ending with the word *svāhā*, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and fuel-sticks combined for the sake of brevity. For this very reason, there is a single deity; thus, the performance is done in a single ritual sequence (*tantra*) for both the curd and the milk, as stated in the *Śrāddhaviveka*: "The curd for Indra on the new moon day, and the milk for Indra on the new moon day. As for what is stated regarding the great gift of the five ploughs (*pañcalāṅgalamahādāna*):
"One should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of milk-rice to Parjanya and the Rudras" (MP 282.7ab).
In a single vessel alone, the Guru should offer to him sacrificial fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, as well as clarified butter and black sesame seeds. (MP 282.7cd–8ab)

Thus, from the *Matsya Purāṇa*: Among the four *hotṛ* priests, whichever one the Guru commands to perform the oblation for Parjanya and the others—that very person should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), *palāśa* wood, clarified butter, and black sesame seeds, each with their respective mantras, to Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras. This has been stated by Bhūpāla and others. That is correct, because of the injunction for the oblation with each individual substance using the two terms "in that same way" (*tadvat*) and "likewise" (*tathā*). For this very reason, after stating "one should offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)" in the *Ratnākara*, the author says "in that same way," meaning one should offer with the *palāśa* wood and so forth. For this very reason, in the rite of the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), Vācaspatimiśra and others have prescribed a single *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation using the combined remnants of the milk-rice from the fire-oblations and the flour-cakes from the Pūṣan-oblation. However, in the case of incapacity:
"In the worship of the planets and so forth, there should be one hundred and eight,
or twenty-eight, or eight, or even according to one's capacity.
From this passage in the *Devīpurāṇa*, indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other numbers should also be mentioned here.
Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the procedure regarding tanks and other such works:
'On all sides of the altar, there should be pits one *aratni* in depth, provided with three tiers. (*MP* 57.4ab; *MP* 57.7cd)
"O Prince, there are nine, seven, or five yoni-mouths," thus he spoke regarding the *kuṇḍas* of nine and so forth.

"Even when [the means] are very small, the rite with a single fire (ekāgni) should be performed by men, provided there is no stinginess regarding wealth" (MP 58.52ef). Based on this observation, they maintain that even here, in the case of incapacity, the rule for a single fire applies. In this instance, the oblation (homa) is to be performed by the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka) alone, according to the statement of Pitāmaha cited in the *Mitākṣarā*. The Adhvaryu priest is merely the sacrificer (yajamāna). Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of the chariot-maker (rathakāra), one must assume the application of specialized knowledge (*vidyā*) for officiating priests from different Vedic branches (*śākhā*); for such an assumption is untenable, since the injunctions prescribe the study of various branches for the Brāhmaṇa alone.
And so Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order..."
"Having remained inviolate in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder" (MDh 3.2). As for the expiatory oblation for the Sāmavedins, it is performed with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
wherever an oblation with the Vyāhṛtis is to serve as an expiation.
In that regard, four [types of women] are to be understood, just as in the case of taking the hand of a woman in marriage. || 127 ||
Alternatively, the oblation to Prajāpati with the mantra "api vā jñātam" may be offered;
this rule for expiation is recorded as having these three options.

Thus, from the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*. However, the *Śāṭyāyanahoma* is not a matter of three alternatives, because that has been refuted by that [text], and because it has been rendered invalid by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa and others. Pitāmaha says:
"Having first weighed the man, and then having lowered him from that... [Pi 97ab]
Facing east and with palms joined in reverence, the judge (prāḍvivāka) should then say:
"Come, come, O Blessed Dharma; enter indeed into this divine ordeal."
Accompanied by the world-protectors, the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts,
one should have that matter written upon a leaf for the person under investigation, and together with this mantra, place it upon his head. (130–131)
The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, and the heart, as well as Yama,
day and night, and both twilights.
For Dharma indeed knows the conduct of a man. (132) One should apply this entire mantra and ritual procedure to all divine ordeals;
likewise, one should perform the invocation of the gods. (133)
The knower of mantras should address the balance with this ritual procedure:
“You, O balance, were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked-minded.
Because of the letter *dha*, you are the embodiment of Dharma; because of the letter *ṭa*, you are the crooked man. [Dhko 482; Pi 100ab–cd]
Because you hold and sustain [the truth], you are therefore called *dhaṭa*.
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
O God, you alone perceive those things which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
(Pi 102cd–103ab) [Pi 103]. The *Nandipurāṇa* describes the manner of writing [the document]:
On an auspicious day and under a favorable lunar mansion, during a propitious zodiacal sign and planetary alignment,
one should have the lords of the gods to be worshipped— Brahmā, Rudra, and Janārdana— inscribed.
Having offered salutation to the eastern direction, being skilled in scripts and the best of scribes, he remains steady in his hands and arms while holding the ink and the leaf. 138.
And from the Matsya Purāṇa:
"He who causes letters to be written that are provided with heads, well-formed, arranged in even rows, and uniform, is considered the supreme scribe. (139)

Thus ends the section on the Ocean of Gifts (*Dānasāgara*). Regarding the reading "dhārayase" (you hold), the variant "bhāvayase" (you cause to exist/manifest) is inappropriate. For, [the verse speaks of] one who is crooked, sinful, or fallen into doubt. In the first case, if he were merely sinful, such a designation would be untenable, as it would imply that even one who is pure attains an upward course. In the second case, since his status is already established, its mention here would be redundant. Therefore, the meaning is simply: "You hold the crooked one"—that is, one accused in legal proceedings. For this very reason, it is stated in the conclusion: "from this doubt," and likewise in the *Smṛtisamuccaya* and *Vyavahāradīpikā*: "therefore, the human being is weighed by you."
Viṣṇu: And he should take up the balance according to the established rule. 140.
And the one who holds the balance.
[Vi 10.7-8] [p.113] The discourse on the Dharma-method is designated as the "Balance" (dhaṭa).
"You alone, O Balance, know those things which human beings do not know. (142) This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with Dharma. (143)
Those worlds that are ordained for slayers of Brahmins, and those worlds for false witnesses—those same worlds belong to the one who holds the scales falsely while weighing. (Vi 10.9)

The meaning is that one should take up and employ the ordeal by balance (*dhaṭa*) according to the rule beginning with "By this rule, you alone, O Balance, know," and likewise employ the weigher of the scale according to the rule beginning with "Those who [are the slayers of Brahmins]," and so forth. Here, among the various mantras composed by different sages which serve the same purpose, there is an option (*vikalpa*)—just as between barley and rice—among those to be recited; however, they are not written here for fear of making the text too voluminous. But for those mantras to be recited by the accused and the judge which have a visible purpose, there is a combination (*samuccaya*). Pitāmaha says: "The ordeals must always be administered to one who is pure and dressed in wet clothes. (145) [Pi 53cd]
"To the pure one," meaning to one who is free from the impurity of birth and death. Regarding wounds, Nārada says in the *Yājñavalkyadīpakālikā*:
"In all cases of hand-wounds, one should make 'swan-foot' marks;
one should observe those very marks on the hands, which are variegated with drops. (146) [N 1.301, YDkā 2.103]

Thus, having marked the wound on the hand of the plaintiff with lac-dye or a similar substance, it must be ascertained whether another wound has occurred or not; therefore, the plaintiff alone has the right to undergo the ordeal by fire. Nārada says:
"For a man who has fasted for a day and night, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes,
the administration of all ordeals is prescribed in the forenoon.
(147) [N 1.268] Furthermore, the *Kālikāpurāṇa* mentions weighing again even prior to the invocation of the balance.

Having first weighed the person who has fasted and bathed against an equal amount of earth on a scale, one should draw a line; then, having lowered him from the scale, one should consecrate him with mantras. — Yājñavalkya.

Weighed by experts skilled in the art of balancing, you have ascended the scale; having been equalized with the counterweight and marked with a line, you have been lowered. O Scale, you are the abode of truth, fashioned of old by the gods.
"Speak that truth, O auspicious one; release me from my doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.101) "If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the scale. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.102)

The accused or the accuser, having been balanced on a scale by merchants and others skilled in weighing with stones and other materials, should—while in that position in which he was balanced during the state of equalization, and having marked with chalk the places where his feet and so forth were situated as well as the ropes of the scale-beams—be removed from the basket and pray to the scale with the mantra: "O Scale, you are Truth; tell, show the true nature of my doubtful matter! The sinner and the liar are unclean, while the pure one is a speaker of truth. This mantra belongs to the *Smṛti* tradition and may be recited even by Śūdras, because the *Smṛti* cited in the *Chandoga-āhnika* states, "For a Śūdra, [everything] except Vedic mantras," due to the specific qualification "Vedic" therein. However, in rites such as the *śrāddha* and the *viśvedevas*, even a *smārta* mantra is prohibited because of the specific injunction of a salutation (*namaskāra*) mantra; the details of this should be investigated in the *Tithitattva*. In the examination of women as well, the mantra should be used exactly as it is, without modification. Since the rule "these ordeals are for purification here" prescribes ordeals for both men and women without distinction, with the result being the removal of doubt regarding a doubtful matter, and since the rule "a human being desires purification" does not allow for modification (*ūha*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), no change is made. For this very reason, it is stated that in the mantra "having girded the wife, [O Agni], come with the clarified butter" (*patnīṃ saṃnahyājyenādehīti*), even when the rite is performed by a sacrificer who has two or many wives, there is no modification to the dual or plural number.

Nārada states that the defendant must hear the meaning of the plaint, which is the matter to be proven: "And he shall cause the accused to hear this matter contained in the document as it is appropriate."
Having caused him to hear [the charge], it should be placed upon his very head and administered in due order.

(152) [N 1.295] The remainder [of the sentence] is that the specific divine ordeal should be administered by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*). Then, he should cause the person to be cleared, with the document placed upon his head, to mount the balance once again.
He should cause him to mount it again, with the document placed upon his head. (153) [Dhko 484]

Thus it is remembered in the Smṛti. A man placed upon a scale [should remain there] for a period of five *vināḍīs*, which is equivalent to the time required to utter three hundred long syllables (*gurvakṣara*).
"O beloved, do not sleep at night in an open space at the end of the fortnight, thinking the lovely, round, and full face [of your lover] to be the moon."
Emaciated by hunger, the cruel Rāhu may seize one here and there;
therefore, in the darkness, one should make one's bed at the edge of the palace.
One should maintain [the vessel] for as long as it takes to recite this verse five times, which amounts to a duration of five *palas*. As the *Smṛti* states:
"An eminent Brāhmaṇa who is an astrologer should perform the examination of the time."
Five *vināḍikās* should be known by those skilled in the determination of the time for examination. And that time is stated in the *Jyotiṣa*:
Ten long syllables constitute one breath (*prāṇa*); six breaths shall be one *vināḍikā*.
Sixty of those should be known as one *ghaṭī*, and sixty *ghaṭikās* likewise constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*).
[Dhko 536] "Likewise" means by sixty.

The Grandfather said: Brāhmaṇas who speak of matters exactly as they have seen them, who are wise, pure, and free from greed—these are the best witnesses; they should indeed be appointed by the king. (157) [Pi 105]
All witnesses declare both purity and impurity before the king in that manner.
(158) [Pi 106] If, when weighed, he should increase in weight, he shall be pure; of this there is no doubt.
[Pi 107ab] If he remains equal or decreases in weight, the man shall not be considered purified. [Dhko 477]

One with minor faults should be known as equal [to the plaintiff], but one with many faults is defeated. (159) [Pi 108] Minor nature [of the fault] may consist in infidelity through embracing and so forth, or in theft through traveling to that person's location and so forth.
Regarding the weighing of these cases, Bṛhaspati says:

If one engaged in the ordeal of the balance is found to have weighed less, he shall suffer loss; but if he is equal, he should be weighed again, and if he has increased in weight, he shall be the victor. (160) [B 8.49] The person to be cleared, having admitted a minor fault, must be weighed again at that very spot for the purpose of determining a major fault. However, if there is a suspicion of a deficiency in the procedure, a different trial must be conducted. Furthermore, when the cutting of the scales or other such parts occurs without any perceptible visible cause, that too constitutes impurity.

In the case of the cutting of the armpit-cloth, the breaking of the balance-beam, as well as the breaking of the *dhaṭa* or the *karkaṭa*, and likewise upon the snapping of the cord or the failure of the axle, one should declare the result to be impure. (161) [B. 8.52]

Thus, from the words of Bṛhaspati: *kakṣa* refers to the bottom of the scale-bag (*śikya*). The two *dhaṭakarkaṭas* are slightly curved iron pins resembling the horns of a crab, serving as supports for the scale-bags at the ends of the balance-beam. According to the *Mitākṣarā* (on Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.102), the *akṣa* is the crossbar fixed upon the two leg-pillars that serves as the support for the balance-beam. Halāyudha states that *dāḍhā* means the pin that acts as the fastener. The *Pārijāta* uses the term *kaṭaka*. However, when their breaking occurs due to a visible cause, one should set the ordeal up again:
"In cases of the cutting or breaking of the scale-bags and other parts, one should set the man up again" (verse 162).
Thus says the Smṛti. And therefore:
He should satisfy the officiating priests, the domestic chaplains, and the teachers with sacrificial fees. Having caused this to be done, the king shall enjoy delightful pleasures. (Pi 79cd–80ab)
He attains great fame and is rendered fit for becoming Brahman. || 163 || [Pi 80cd]

The judge, preceded by salutations to the world-protectors (lokapālas) and others, shall construct the balance according to the described characteristics. Then, having erected two pillars six cubits high, he should bury them two cubits deep in the southern and northern directions with a separation of two cubits between them. Upon the tops of these pillars, which hold the cross-beam (paṭṭa), he should place a cross-beam provided with holes at the center and on both sides, and fixed with an iron hook (lauhāṅkuśa) inserted in the middle. He should then join that beam to the iron ring at the center of the balance using the hook situated in the middle. Thus, the horizontal beam of the balance stands between the two pillars. He should then secure the ropes for the two scale-pans (śikya) to two iron pins fixed at the ends of the beam. On the eastern and western sides of the balance, two gateway-pillars (toraṇastambha) ten finger-breadths higher than the beam should be made. Above the gateways, two downward-facing earthen suspensions, connected by a cord and touching the top of the balance, should be fashioned. Just as the lowering and raising of the balance are to be known from the displacement of the suspensions, so too they are to be known by means of water.
Now follows the ritual application of this.

Having observed a fast and performed his ablutions and other rites, the Brahmin judge shall inquire into the case and examine what has been reported. Then, having weighed the accused and removed him from the scale, he should perform the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and so forth. Having uttered "Oṃ tat sat," he should worship three Brahmins with perfumes and other offerings, and cause each of them to recite three times, "May there be an auspicious day for this rite of examination, may there be well-being, and may there be success. Then, for the sake of the *homa* which is a constituent part of the ordeal, he should honor and appoint four Brahmins as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) with water for the feet and other honors; if unable to do so, he may appoint one Brahmin and one officiating priest. Then, having placed a level balance adorned with a flag upon the ground, he should stand facing east upon it, take flowers and unbroken rice grains, and utter: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and then "Oṃ."
Come, come, O Blessed One, Dharma; indeed, enter into this divine [image], together with the guardians of the world and the hosts of Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts.

Having invoked Dharma with this mantra, one should offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, *madhuparka*, *punarācamanīya*, bathing water, garments, sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), crown, and other ornaments up to the end of the decorations, using the formula: "This is the *arghya* for Dharma; *oṃ* obeisance to Dharma," and so forth. In the same manner, one should worship [Dharma] from the *arghya* through the ornaments, using his respective name preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *namaḥ*. To Indra in the east; to Yama in the south; to Varuṇa in the west; to Kubera in the north; to Agni in the southeast; to Nairṛti in the southwest; to Vāyu in the northwest; and to Īśāna in the northeast. To the eight Vasus individually on the right side of Indra, each with their own names.
The meditation on the Vasus is described in the Ādityapurāṇa:
"They have serene faces, are gentle, grant boons, and hold tridents in their hands."
The eight Vasus are proclaimed to be seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and possessing two arms. || 165 ||

There, [one should worship] Dharā, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa. Between Indra and Īśāna, likewise, [one should worship] the twelve Ādityas. Their meditation is described in the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "Seated upon lotus-thrones, two-armed, with the luster of the interior of a lotus, they hold blue lotuses extending from their hands up to their shoulders."
The twelve Ādityas, beginning with Dhātṛ, are situated in the midst of the orb of light.

There, [offerings are made] to Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, Bhaga, Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu. To the west of Agni, likewise, there are eleven for the Rudras. Regarding their meditation, it is said in the Ādityapurāṇa:
"Carrying tridents in their left hands and rosaries in their right hands, the eleven Rudras should be fashioned with three eyes and the crescent moon upon their crests. (167)

There, one should worship Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Giriśa, Aje-kapāda, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, Aparājita, Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālin, Sthāṇu, and Bhava; likewise, between Yama and Rakṣas, the Mothers (Mātṛs). Therein, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā. To the north of Nirṛti, Gaṇeśa; to the north of Varuṇa, the eight Maruts. Therein, Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, Māruta, Prāṇa, Prāneśa, and Jīva. On the northern part of the balance, Durgā. Having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings to Dharma as before, one should present perfumes and other articles to those beginning with Indra and ending with Durgā. Then, in the four directions, four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) shall establish four fires—or, if unable, a single priest shall do so—having established a single fire according to the domestic ritual (*gṛhya*) prescribed by the Chief Justice (*prāḍvivāka*). Having recited the *Gāyatrī* mantra enclosed by the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*), accompanied by the *Vyāhṛtis*, and ending with *svāhā*, he should offer one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight oblations of clarified butter, milk, and fuel-sticks combined. For the Sāma-singers, however, the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) is performed with the *Mahāvyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively. Then he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having thus completed the worship of the deities up to the oblation, he should give the fee. Then, having placed the person to be tested (*śodhya*), who has fasted and is wearing wet clothes, on the western scale pan, and having placed a brick on the eastern pan, he should lift them and, having determined equality by pouring water onto the balance, he should lower them. Then the Chief Justice, using a line of equal number of syllables in two rows, [should apply] the lamp-oil from that day’s soot to her [the plaintiff's] eyelashes, free from interruption.
The sun and the moon, the wind and the fire, heaven, earth, water, and the heart, as well as Yama,
day and night, and both twilights— Dharma indeed knows the conduct of a man. (168) [Pi 78]

Having thus written upon the document a plaint consisting of forty-four syllables, which takes the form of performing or not performing the intended purpose and includes such statements as "this debt was given to him" or "this debt was not received by me from him," and having placed that document upon the head of the person to be examined, the specific manner of writing has been performed in accordance with the *Paddhati* of Hari-hara and the *Vyavahāradīpikā*. Thereafter, the judge should address the balance with these words:
"O Balance, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked."
From the letter *dha* you are the embodiment of Dharma; from the letter *ṭa*, you are the crooked man.
Because you hold and maintain [the truth], you are therefore called *Dhaṭa*.
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings.
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not understand; this man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification.
Therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with Dharma.
One should restrain the weigher with this mantra:
"Those worlds that are ordained for the slayers of Brahmins, and those worlds for false witnesses—those same worlds shall belong to the weigher who holds the scales falsely. [Vi 10.9]
Then the accused person should address the balance with this:
"O Balance, you are the abode of truth, fashioned of old by the gods."
"Speak that truth, O auspicious one; release me from my doubt.
(174) [Y 2.101] "If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward; if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the scale. (175) [Y 2.102]

Then the judge shall cause him to mount the balance as before, facing the east. Once he has mounted it, he should leave him there for a period of five *palas* to determine his innocence or guilt. Then, if the balance remains higher than its counterweight, he is innocent; if it remains lower, he is guilty; and even if it remains level, he is slightly at fault. One should declare him guilty if there is a breakage or fracture in the side-arms, the pins, the hooks, the sling, the feet, the axle, or other parts—provided it is not due to a visible external cause. Thereafter, he should satisfy the officiating priest, the teacher, and others with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Now follows the trial by fire.
I shall proclaim the rite of the fire exactly as it is spoken in the scriptures.
One should cause eight mandalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth.
The first mandala is that of Agni, while the second is known as that of Varuṇa.
The third has Vāyu as its deity, and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth has Indra as its deity, and the sixth is said to belong to Kubera.
The seventh has Soma as its deity, and likewise the eighth belongs to Savitṛ.
Those who know the divine know that the ninth belongs to all the deities;
and they know that which is the ninth in front to be the great earthly one. (179) [Dhko 495]
"Great earthly" means having an unlimited number of finger-breadths.
They should be made with cow dung and sprinkled with water. They say that the distance between the mandalas is thirty-two finger-breadths. (Pi 112cd–113)

With eight mandalas, there are thus two hundred and fifty-six finger-breadths; such is the calculation for the ground. The mandala should be made equal in measure to the foot of the practitioner. (181–182) [Pi 114–115]

"Āgneya" means having Agni as its deity; the same applies elsewhere. By that [designation], Agni and the others are to be worshipped by him. The mandala is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and the space between them is also sixteen finger-breadths, making thirty-two finger-breadths in total.
And so says Yājñavalkya: "The mandala should be known as sixteen finger-breadths, and the interval should be of the same measure. (YDh 2.106cd)
Thus it is said: "In every mandala, kusha grasses should be provided as enjoined by the scriptures;
one should always place one's foot upon them—this is the established rule. [Pi 116]
Then, facing eastward, he should stand with his hands outstretched in the *añjali* gesture;
wearing wet clothes and being pure, he should place a leaf upon his head.
He should stand in the western mandala facing east, pure and with palms joined in reverence.
They would observe the wounds and other marks on the hands of that perpetrator;
[this refers to] him whose grain has been seized.

And so says Yājñavalkya: "Having marked the two hands after they have been rubbed with rice grains, one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread. (YDh 2.103)

The phrase "of one whose rice-grains have been crushed" implies "with both hands. Having marked the hands of one whose rice-grains have been crushed, one should mark them at the locations of scars, moles, and the like with drops of red sandalwood paste and other substances in the form of lines shaped like *haṃsapada* (swan-foot) figures.
Thus says Nārada:
"In all cases of hand-scars, one should indeed fashion *haṃsapadas*."
Furthermore, one should observe those very hands, adorned with drops.
Then, upon the hands, one should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha*, seven leaves of the *śamī*, seven leaves of the *dūrvā*, barley grains mixed with curd, and flowers.
Next, in due order, seven leaves of the *pippala* and *śamī*.
"One should place seven leaves of *dūrvā* grass smeared with curd, along with unbroken grains (*akṣata*)," according to the verse cited in the *Mitākṣarā*:
"Seven leaves of the *pippala* tree, unbroken grains, flowers, and curd."
"One should place them there and likewise wrap them with thread," according to the statement of Pitāmaha (Yājñavalkya).
Nārada further specifies the type of thread:
One should wrap both hands with seven threads of white cotton. 191.
[Dhko 490] Likewise, [p.127]
A blacksmith who is skilled by birth in the work of fire and has seen its application elsewhere should heat iron in the fire until it becomes a glowing mass of iron,
emitting sparks and beautifully colored.
Having had another [weight] of fifty *palas* prepared, the pure twice-born man, while the [accused] is undergoing the third heating, should address him with the "preface of truth" (*satyapuraskṛta*).
The term "preface of truth" means accompanied by the word "truth"; the meaning is that he should recite the mantra spoken by Yājñavalkya beginning with: "O Agni, you [are the witness] of all beings."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) specifies the iron ball:
having fashioned it from iron, free from flaws, measuring eight finger-breadths, one should heat the ball, weighing fifty palas, evenly in the fire. [Pi 121]
The corner is the *asra*. As for the measurement of a finger (*aṅgula*):
eight horizontal barley grains or three vertical rice grains is said to be the measure of a finger; twelve fingers is a *vitasti*. [Dhko 534]
Manu states the measure of a *pala*:
"Five *kṛṣṇalas* make a *māṣa*; sixteen of those make a *suvarṇa*;
four *suvarṇas* make a *pala*. (MDh 8.134cd–135a)
Thus, according to that worldly measure, twenty palas measuring eight *tolakas* each, plus six *tolakas*, five *māṣakas*, and four *rattikas*, result from fifty Vedic *palas*.
Thereafter: "For the sake of pacification, one should offer ghee into the fire one hundred and eight times. (198) [Dhko 496]

Thus, according to the *Mitākṣarā*: the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka), having established the fire on the southern side of the sacrificial ground (*maṇḍalabhūmi*) according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, shall offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra stated in the *Mitākṣarā*: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni Pāvaka. Then, having heated that iron ball (*lauha-piṇḍa*) in that fire, having cast it into water, and having heated it again and cast it into water once more, he should perform the previously mentioned procedure beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the oblation. He should then consecrate the fire residing within the ball with these mantras recited by the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and others, beginning with: "Oṃ..."
O Agni, you are the four Vedas, and you are invoked in the sacrifices;
you are the mouth of all the gods, and you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman.
For, dwelling within the bellies of living beings, you therefore know both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Because you indeed purify evil, therefore you are called Pāvaka (the Purifier).
O Pāvaka, manifest yourself among the wicked and become radiant;
or else, among those of pure disposition, be cool, O Hūtāśana (Consumer of Oblations)!
O Agni, you move within all living beings like a witness;
O God, you alone know those things which human beings do not know. (202) [Pi 126] This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification.
Therefore, you ought to protect him from this doubt in accordance with the Dharma.

(203) [Pi 127] [p.129] Then, having placed seven *aśvattha* leaves upon the hands of the two who have been prepared by the crushing of rice, and having bound them with seven threads, the judge, standing within the primary mandala, should consecrate the iron ball brought forward by the messenger with this mantra spoken by Yājñavalkya.
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
O Sage, like a witness, speak the truth regarding my merits and sins. 204. [Y 2.104]

The meaning of this is as follows: O Agni, you move within the bodies of all beings—whether born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from a sprout; you exist as the digester of the food and drink consumed, or rather, you know that which is in the heart of everyone. O Pāvaka, the cause of purification; O Kavi, the inner-seer, that is to say, the omniscient one. Therefore, like a witness, speak the truth regarding merits and demerits. The ablative case in "puṇyapāpebhyaḥ" is used with the elision of a verbal suffix (lyap), meaning: having observed the merits and demerits, speak the truth—that is, reveal it. Following that, Yājñavalkya [spoke].
When he has spoken thus, the king or the judge shall place upon both his hands a smooth iron ball weighing fifty palas and heated to the color of fire.
[Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.105] "He shall place" means the king or the presiding judge.
Just as the Grandfather [Manu] has prescribed:
"Then, having taken hold of him, the king devoted to dharma, using a pair of tongs or with his own hands, should place him upon the scales. (206) [Pi 128]
That iron ball. Appointed refers to the judge. Of this person performing the ordeal. Yājñavalkya.
Taking that [water], he should walk slowly for exactly seven *maṇḍalas*.
[Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.106ab] By the word "single" (*eka*), both the placement of the foot upon the *maṇḍalas* and the crossing over the *maṇḍalas* are indicated.
Pitāmaha has stated this clearly:
One should not step beyond the mandala, nor should one place a foot within it;
having reached the eighth mandala, the wise man should step onto the ninth. (Kālikāpurāṇa 129cd–130ab)

Likewise, there are seven mandalas, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in size. One should proceed by intervals of that same measure; having gone [that distance], one should cast [the flower] onto the ninth blade of grass.
And here, it is not contradictory because one must traverse exactly seven mandalas, since one stands at the first and casts [the flower] at the ninth.
Yājñavalkya:
"If the *piṇḍa* falls in between, or if there is doubt, one should offer it again" (2.107cd).

"In case of doubt" means when there is doubt as to whether it has been burnt or not. One should offer it again by placing the *piṇḍa* once more within that same ritual performance and completing the remainder; however, this does not constitute a separate ritual performance, because the injunction specifies only the re-offering of what was being offered, and because it remains uncertain whether the original performance has become defective.

Kātyāyana says: If one who is under accusation stumbles and is burned elsewhere than at the designated spot, the gods consider him not burned; he shall be made to undergo the ordeal once more. (211) [K 441]
Yājñavalkya says: Having released the fire and having softened grains of rice without burning them, he shall attain purification. (2.107ab)
Nārada: One should grind rice with great care for seven nights. Pitāmaha: [as above].

If, while they are massaging with their hands without hesitation, no change occurs at the end of the day, one should declare that person to be pure. (214) [Pi 131] Now follows the performance of the fire ordeal.

On the previous day, having performed the purification of the ground, on the following day, as before, one should prepare eight mandalas each measuring sixteen *aṅgulas*, with the intervening spaces also measuring sixteen *aṅgulas*, and the ninth mandala of an unlimited number of *aṅgulas*. Having spread out iron hooks (*aṅkuśa*) pointing eastward upon them, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), taking red flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) in the first mandala, should invoke and establish [the deity] with the mantra: *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, Agne, come here, stay here!* and worship him with perfumes and other offerings. In the same manner, he should worship Varuṇa in the second, Vāyu in the third, Yama in the fourth, Indra in the fifth, Kubera in the sixth, Soma in the seventh, Sūrya in the eighth, and all the deities in the ninth. Then, having established the fire to the south of the mandalas according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, he should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) one hundred and eight times with clarified butter using the mantra: *Oṃ agnaye pāvakāya svāhā*. Then, in that fire, he should heat an iron ball (*lauhapinda*)—measuring one hundred and sixty-six *tolakas* plus five *māṣakas* and four *rattikas* by common measure, eight *aṅgulas* in size, and free from any corners—and plunge it into water. Having heated it again and plunged it again, and heating it once more, he should perform upon that ball the entire ritual for the deities as prescribed for the balance (*tulā*), beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the oblation, and then give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having approached the defendant—who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes—standing in the first mandala, the judge should perform the ritual purification of the hand by rubbing it with rice. He should bind the written pledge (*pratijñāpatra*) together with the mantras to the head of the litigant. Then, during the third heating, the judge should consecrate the fire contained within the iron ball with these [mantras]:
Oṃ!
You, O Agni, are the four Vedas; you are invoked in the sacrifices.
You are the mouth of all the gods; you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman. 215. [Pi 123]
For, dwelling within the bellies of all beings, you therefore know their good and evil;
since you indeed purify sin, you are called Pāvaka (the Purifier).
O Pāvaka, manifest yourself among the wicked and become radiant with flames!
Or rather, O Fire, become cool through your pure nature.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
you alone, O God, know those things which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with the Dharma.

Then, having placed seven *aśvattha* leaves, seven *śamī* leaves, seven *dūrvā* leaves, barley grains mixed with curd, and flowers upon the hands of the performer, he should wrap them seven times with a white thread. The performer should consecrate the fire contained within the iron ball with this mantra:
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, speak the truth to me regarding my merits and sins. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.104)

Then one should place an iron ball upon his hands. Then, taking it, he should walk slowly and straightly through seven circles in succession and drop it upon the grass situated within the ninth circle. Thereafter, he should again rub his hands with rice grains. If it is not burnt, he attains purification. If the ball falls midway, or if there is doubt as to whether it is burnt or unburnt, he should take it up again. In the event of a stumble, there is no fault even if there is burning elsewhere on the hands. Then he should satisfy the preceptor, the family priest, and others with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Now follows the examination by water. Pitāmaha says:
Now I shall proclaim the righteous and eternal ritual for the water-offering (toyāñjali).
A wise person should cause a mandala to be prepared with flowers and incense.
One should worship the arrows and likewise the bamboo bow with devotion.
Among those, first one should worship Varuṇa,
as Nārada has stated:
First, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the worship of Varuṇa with fragrant perfumes and garlands, honey, milk, clarified butter, and other such offerings. Then,

one should perform the ritual beginning with the invocation of Dharma (dharmāvāhana) and ending with the placement of the document of commitment (pratijñāpatra) upon the head, including the worship of all the deities and the fire-oblation (homa) accompanied by mantras.
Kātyāyana says: For the sake of purification, one should make arrows with tips not made of iron;
the thrower should cast bamboo, wood, or fibers very firmly. (223) [K 442]
The grandfather says: A Kṣatriya who is capable of hurling [the weapon] should be appointed, or else a Brāhmaṇa who follows that same occupation;
