he must be gentle-hearted, tranquil, fasting, and likewise pure. (224) [Pi 141]
A wise man should not discharge an arrow when the wind blows violently,
nor on uneven ground crowded with trees and stumps.
— Nārada.
A cruel bow is seven hundred [finger-breadths] in measure; a medium one is known to be six hundred;

a mild one is declared to be five hundred. This is to be understood as the rule for bows. (226) [N 1.307] That bow whose measurement is one hundred and seven finger-breadths is "seven-hundred"; likewise for "six-hundred" and so forth.
The Grandfather said:
"But with the middle bow, one should discharge three arrows."
Having set a target at a distance of one hundred and fifty *hasta*s, the wise man,
according to the instructions of the treatises, should have arrows shot; then,
among those discharged arrows, a strong man must catch the middle one.
One should grasp the falling of the arrows and avoid their gliding;
for as the arrow glides and glides, it goes from a distance to an even greater distance.

(229) [Pi 146] The phrase "the falling should be grasped" means that one should go as far as the place where the arrow falls. Therefore, even in the case of the gliding [arrow], one must grasp the arrow at the point of its fall; consequently, first of all, another person must bring an arrow to that spot.
Nārada said: One should perform the immersion of men in rivers that are not too swift, and in tanks, lakes, and ponds with still waters. (230) [N 1.305]
Nor in waters that are too deep, nor in those where stability is compromised and devoid of current.
Viṣṇu says:
[One should bathe] in water free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like. (Vi 12.2)
While he is submerged in water reaching up to his navel, free from passion and hatred, another person should seize his thighs and enter the consecrated water.
Simultaneously, another person should discharge an arrow from a bow that is neither too stiff nor too soft.

The meaning is "of that person to be purified"; otherwise, the word *tasya* would be redundant. The *Smṛti* states that another person shall hold the pillar: "He should stand in the water facing the east, grasping the pillar of Dharma" (234). Pitāmaha describes the consecration of the water performed by the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*):
O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings and were fashioned as the first creation;
you are declared to be the cause of purification for substances as well as for embodied beings.
Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Yājñavalkya states regarding the consecration performed by the person undergoing purification:
"Having sworn, 'O Varuṇa, protect me by truth,' while standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should seize the thighs and enter the water. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.108)

"May he not [enter] me"—having thus caused him to swear an oath—[the accused] shall enter the water, that is, submerge himself. And near the place of immersion, on level ground, a *toraṇa* (archway) should be erected to a height equal to the ear of the person undergoing the ordeal.
As Nārada says:
"Having gone to that body of water, one should erect an archway on its bank."
One should make a mark the size of a span on a level and pure patch of ground.
Regarding the specific rule for discharging the arrow, Nārada and Bṛhaspati say:
from the spot where the arrow is released, a young man endowed with speed—
One should go with the utmost speed to where that middle arrow has fallen.
Then, another man of similar capacity, taking up the middle arrow,
should return with great velocity from the place where that first man went.
But when the arrow-retriever who has come does not clearly see what is situated within the water, then one should declare purification. (241)
Otherwise, it would not be pure, even if one single part were seen;
whether from its place or by moving elsewhere, one should first establish that in which Nārada distinguishes the two swift ones.
"Of the fifty runners, those two who possess superior speed should be appointed there for the purpose of fetching the arrow;
this is because even from the sight of a single limb," and so on, referring to the ear and other parts.
"Only the head is seen, neither the ears nor the nose;
one should declare that person also pure if they have entered the water"—
this is because of this specific statement.

If a person who has been bitten by a living creature sinks and then floats up, he should be considered as having been bitten by that very creature if he sinks again at that spot. (245) [Dhko 503] The meaning is: one who has been bitten by a fish, leech, or similar creature within the water floats up; therefore, when bitten, one must sink once more.
The Grandfather said:
"For both the one who goes and the one who performs the rite, the journey and the immersion are equal."

A swift man should go from the base of the archway to the place where the arrow lies. When he has gone there, a second man, also taking up an arrow, should go with speed to the base of the archway from which that first man departed.
But when the outsider who holds the arrow does not clearly see what has entered the water, then one should declare purification. [Pi 144]

In this context, the statement by Śūlapāṇi that the movement [of the person] occurs at the same time as the discharge of the arrow is incorrect, because it contradicts the description of the movement occurring simultaneously with the immersion. Furthermore, the alternative statement—that one should take up the middle arrow which was discharged at the same time as the immersion—is also devoid of authoritative evidence. Therefore, the meaning of the circular procedure is as follows: when three arrows have been discharged, one swift person goes to the place where the middle arrow falls, takes it, and remains right there. While the two of them remain thus stationed, on the third clap of hands given by the judge (*praḍvivāka*), the person undergoing purification (*śodhya*) immerses himself. At that very same moment, the other person standing at the base of the archway also runs even more swiftly to the place where the middle arrow fell. When the arrow-retriever reaches that spot, he returns even more swiftly to the base of the archway; if he does not see the person who had gone into the water, then he is declared pure. This is the sense of the entire passage.

Therein, the procedure is as follows: having erected a gateway (toraṇa) near a body of water possessing the characteristics previously described, and having fixed the target in the prescribed place; having placed a bow with an arrow near the gateway; having invoked and worshipped Varuṇa in the body of water; and having worshipped the deities beginning with Dharma on its bank up to the end of the fire-oblation (havana), and having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); the judge, having tied the document of the oath upon the head of the person to be purified, shall consecrate the water with the mantra:
*Oṃ*.
O Water, you are the life-breath of living beings and were fashioned as the first creation;
you are declared to be the cause of purification for substances as well as for embodied beings.
Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of what is auspicious and what is inauspicious.

With this mantra; the person undergoing the ordeal, however, having consecrated the water with the mantra “Oṃ, protect me by truth, O Varuṇa,” shall go into the midst of the water toward a strong man facing east who has grasped a pillar and is standing in water reaching up to his navel. Then, after three arrows have been discharged and one swift man is stationed at the spot where the middle arrow fell while holding that middle arrow, and another is stationed at the base of the archway, the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka) gives three claps of his hands. At that signal, the person undergoing the ordeal, having grasped the thighs of the man facing east who holds the pillar, submerges himself. Simultaneously, the man at the base of the archway also moves quickly away. Then, when the person has reached the spot, the arrow-retriever quickly reaches the base of the archway; if he does not see the person inside the water, then he is purified. Even if only the head is visible without the ears or other limbs, he is purified. He should then give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth.
Now follows the procedure for poison. Nārada says:
That which comes from the Śārṅga mountain or the Himavat is recommended, provided it is endowed with the proper fragrance, color, and taste.
That which is natural, even, hidden, and not impaired by mantras;
[Dhko 507] [p.140] the measure is four barley-corns in the rainy season, and five barley-corns is prescribed for the summer.
In the winter there should be seven barley grains, and in the autumn even fewer than that. Having fasted, one should offer two beans in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
after having worshipped Maheśvara with incense, offerings, and mantras.
In the presence of the twice-born, while standing facing south,
a Brahmin, composed in mind, should give [the gift] facing either north or east.
(254) [Dhko 508] Kātyāyana describes the form of the Śārṅga bow:

The poison known as Śṛṅgiṇa originates from a horn; it resembles the horn of a goat, is dark in color, very cold, and when broken, it has the appearance of ginger. It turns blood black and makes it hard instantly.

*Śṛṅgavera* is *ārdraka*; "resembling that" means equal to it. "Situated in the blood" (*raktastha*) means that poison which has been placed in the blood; the meaning is that it makes that blood dark and solid. "Small" (*alpa*) means the size of six barley grains (*ṣaḍyava*). By the mention of "winter" (*hemanta*), the "cool season" (*śiśira*) is also included, according to the Vedic tradition that winter and the cool season have the same end. Since spring is common to all divine [seasons], Yājñavalkya has stated generally regarding that as well: "seven barley grains, or seven [units] of poison" (Y 2.98d). Kātyāyana says:
In the forenoon, in a cool place, poison should be administered to the litigants;
it should be finely ground and mixed with thirty times its amount of clarified butter.
This is to be administered by the presiding judge.
Regarding that which is to be recited, the Grandfather said: "Having taken the poison in his hand while it is being given, he should administer the oath. (257) [Pi 151]
O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the evil-minded;
show yourself to the sinners, but become nectar for those who are pure.
O Poison, embodiment of death, you have indeed been fashioned by Brahmā.
"Save this man from evil; by truth, become nectar for him.
[Pi 153] One should cause him to swear—that is, one should make him take an oath.
Yājñavalkya states the procedure for the person to be cleared of suspicion:

"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in the dharma of truth. Protect me from this curse; by the power of truth, become nectar for me! (260) Having spoken thus once, he should consume the Śārṅga poison produced from the snowy mountains. (261ab)
The Grandfather said: "When, after consuming it, he is well, free from fainting or dizziness, and remains without any physical change at the end of the day, one should designate him as pure. [Pi 156]

For three nights or five nights, the king should have the person undergoing the ordeal guarded by his own men; out of fear of trickery and the like, he should prevent the performer of the ordeal from using medicinal herbs, mantra-applications, or gems that neutralize poison. (263) [Pi 154] He should likewise forbid the use of antidotes to poison.
One should examine those born in secret for physical characteristics that resemble those of their maker.

In the science of poisons (*viṣatantra*), the first impulse produced by poison causes horripilation, fainting, and so forth, as well as perspiration and salivation; the two following it produce discoloration and trembling in the body; the fifth impulse brings about a distressing state of the eyes and a breaking pain in the throat; the sixth bestows hiccup, labored breathing, and delusion; and the seventh brings death to the consumer. [p.142]

Bṛhaspati: He who has swallowed poison given according to the prescribed rule, even without the recitation of mantras, shall be deemed pure; otherwise, however, he is to be punished and made to pay that wealth. [B 8.64]
Now, the procedure for this is as follows:

The judge, having fasted, shall worship Śiva and, in his presence, place the aforementioned quantity of ground poison mixed with thirty times its weight of clarified butter. Having performed the rites from the invocation of Dharma and the other deities up to the oblation (*havana*), and having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he shall place the written confession upon the head of the person to be purified, saying "Oṃ."
"O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked;
manifest yourself before sinners, but become nectar for those who are pure.
O Poison, embodiment of death, you have indeed been fashioned by Brahmā. [Pi 152]

"Save this man from evil; by truth, let there be immortality for him. (259) [Pi 153] Having thus consecrated the poison while facing either the east or the north, he gives it to the person to be purified, who faces the south. As for the person to be purified:
Oṃ!
You, Poison, are the son of Brahmā, established in the dharma of truth. Protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me. 260. [Y 2.110]
Having consecrated it with this mantra, he consumes it. If, until the end of the day, there is no change, then he is pure.
Now follows the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa).

Nārada says: The drinking of the ordeal-substance (koṣapāna) is prescribed for one who has fasted in the forenoon, who has bathed and put on a wet garment, who possesses the śūka-grass, and who is free from vice.
A wise person should not give a gift to one who desires it with faith in the presence of gods and Brahmins,
nor to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers,
nor likewise to those who follow the conduct of atheists.

One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the vessel (koṣapāna) in the case of those who have committed a great offense, those devoid of dharma, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, atheists, those who have not undergone the initiatory rites (vrātya),
and slaves. Having summoned the accused, however, one should place him within the circle.
Having turned him toward the sun, one should have him drink three handfuls.
For if a great abnormality should occur after seven days,
he must not be employed by the wise man, because the appointed time has passed.

"Conscientious" (*saśūka*) means one who believes in the afterlife (*āstika*), according to the *Mitākṣarā*. "A great offender" (*mahāparādhin*) is one who has committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*). "Devoid of merit" (*nirdharma*) means one who lacks the status of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramarahita*). "Despised" (*kutsita*) refers to one born of an inverse marriage (*pratilomaja*). "Servant" (*dāsa*) refers to a fisherman (*kaivarta*). "Within the circle" (*maṇḍalābhyantare*) means within a circle made of cow dung. "Abnormality" (*vaikṛta*) refers to disease and the like. It is "great" and not small, because it is unavoidable for embodied beings. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Now, in case of a discrepancy with fate, one should cause [the fine] to be paid after two weeks."
One should apply effort toward that goal and likewise toward punishment for it;
if that were to happen to that single individual and not to all people.
Disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, debt, and the imposition of a fine— these are the consequences;
likewise, fever, dysentery, eruptive boils, pain in the hidden bones,
eye disease, throat disease, and insanity arise.
Headache and arm-palsy are divine diseases for men.

[276] [K 458] Regarding "throat disease" (*galaroga*), in some places the reading is "piercing pain" (*śūlaroga*). However, the period of two weeks refers to the subject of major charges (*mahābhiyoga*); for, having introduced the topic with "these [ordeals] apply to major charges" [Y 2.95c], Yājñavalkya states "up to the fourteenth day" [Y 2.113a]. The *Mitākṣarā* explains it in this same way.
As for that which...
"Whether after three nights, seven nights, twelve days, or fourteen days, he in whom a physical abnormality (*vaikṛta*) is observed is declared a doer of evil. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.113).

Regarding this statement by Pitāmaha, the *Mitākṣarā* explains that for a major ordeal (*mahābhiyoga*), the property involved should be divided into three portions, and the three periods of three nights and so forth should be established accordingly, depending on whether the value of the property is less than the full amount.
Likewise:

"One should have that person drink the water belonging to whichever deity he is devoted to; but if there is no partiality toward any particular deity, one should have him drink the water of Āditya. [Pi 157]
One should cause thieves and those who live by the sword to drink the water of Durgā;
however, one should not cause a Brāhmaṇa to drink that water which belongs to Bhāskara. 279.
One should bathe the trident of Durgā and the maṇḍala of Āditya;
likewise, one should bathe the weapons of the other gods as well. [Pi 159] Regarding this:

"Upon a minor offense, having bathed him with the water used for the gods' weapons, he should be made to drink it; if he is impure due to a major transgression, he shall be restrained; otherwise, if he is pure, [he is released].

Because of this specific rule stated by Kātyāyana, there is a distinction of scope: the "water used for bathing the gods" applies to a major offense. Ratnākara also says the same. The *Vyavahāradīpikā* states that the *maṇḍala* is the sky (*vyoman*); in that [work], Viṣṇu says:
Having worshipped the fierce deities, he should drink three handfuls of the water used for their ablutions (282).
Facing the deities and declaring, "This has not been done by me," (283)—
it is according to this very principle that the vow mentioned previously is applied elsewhere.
The procedure here is as follows:

the presiding judge, having performed within a circle made of cow-dung all the rites beginning with the invocation of Dharma and ending with the oblation (*havana*)—including the worship of all the deities—and having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), shall place the written confession along with its mantras upon the head of the person to be purified; then, having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rules and brought that water used for bathing [the image], [he shall proceed].
Oṃ!
You, O Water, are the life-force of living beings, fashioned as the primordial creation;
you are declared to be the cause of purity for embodied beings as well as for all fluids. [Pi 139]
"Therefore, reveal yourself for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious.

(284) [Pi 140] Having consecrated [the water] with these two [mantras], he should cause the person to be purified—who stands within a mandala made of cow dung, who has fasted, whose garments are still wet from bathing, and who faces the sun—to drink three handfuls of water consecrated by the person to be purified reciting: "O Varuṇa, protect me by truth! (*oṃ satyena mābhirakṣasva varuṇa*). Then, if no affliction such as illness occurs within the fixed period of time, he is pure. Thereafter, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given.
Now follows the procedure for rice (*taṇḍula-vidhi*).
The Grandfather says: "In cases of theft, however, rice grains are to be administered; this is the settled rule.
One should have the rice grains made from white *śāli* rice, and not from any other kind."

Having placed them in an earthen vessel before the Sun, being pure, he should let them remain there that very night, mixed with bath-water. [Pi 164cd–165ab] He should be facing east, having fasted, bathed, and with leaves placed upon his head. [Pi 166ab]
Having eaten rice grains, one should spit them out three times onto a leaf—specifically on that of the *bhūrja* tree, and not on any other; however, in its absence, on that of the *pippala*.
[If] blood is seen [in the spittle], and his jaw and palate become parched, [then he is in danger]. 287–288ab.
One whose body trembles should be designated as impure.
(288) [Pi 168cd] "With bathing water" means with the water used for bathing a deity. And likewise, Kātyāyana says:

One who bathes in the water used for the deities' ablutions, drinks it, or eats unhusked rice that has been moistened by it becomes pure by spitting it out; otherwise, he is impure and must be restrained. [K 453]

One who has placed a leaf upon his head should chew rice grains and spit them out. Regarding the term *prāḍvivāka*, it is explained as "one who causes [the accused] to spit" (*niṣṭhīvayet*), derived from the causative form of the root. Furthermore, the common procedure for all ordeals—from the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) up to the oblation (*havana*)—must be performed here as well, just as previously described.
Now follows the rule for the ordeal of the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣa*). Pitāmaha says:
One should have a vessel made of iron or copper measuring sixteen finger-breadths,
or else a circular mandala made of clay with a hollow four finger-breadths deep.
(290) [Pi 170] "Mandala" means circular, in the shape of the solar disc.
One should fill it with twenty palas of ghee and oil;
then, once it is well-heated, one should cast a gold māṣaka into it.
Using the thumb and finger together, one should extract the heated māṣaka.
He whose fingertips do not shake, or upon whom no eruption appears,
becomes pure through the Dharma, according to the word of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
[Pi 173] He states another ritual procedure:
Having taken cow’s ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
[Pi 174] One should take a well-purified ladle made of gold, silver, copper, or iron.
One should cast the ring there, having washed it once with water,
into that place rich with swirling ripples and waves, which is beyond the reach of the touch of fingernails.
One should examine it with a fresh leaf, making a sucking sound accompanied by noise.
Then, one should consecrate it once with this mantra:
"O ghee, you are the supreme purifier and nectar in sacrificial rites."
"O purifier, may you become more purifying; O cool as snow, be hot in the heat!
(298). Then, once she has fasted, bathed, and returned wearing wet clothes, he should have her take that ring while it is submerged in ghee. (299)
Then, the examiners should examine his ring finger;
he whose eruptions do not appear is pure, otherwise he is impure. (300) [Pi 180] The ritual application is as follows:

In a vessel made of copper or other metals—or, if such materials are unavailable, one made of clay—shaped circularly like a wheel, with a width of sixteen fingers (where one finger-measure consists of eight barley grains of medium size), and a depth of four such fingers, one should pour either clarified butter (*ghṛta*) weighing ten *vedika-palas* (equivalent to thirty-three *tolakas* plus two *māṣakas* plus eight worldly *raktikas), or likewise oil; or else, one may pour pure cow’s milk weighing twenty *vedika-palas* (equivalent to sixty-six *tolakas* plus five *māṣakas* plus four worldly *raktikas*). Once that has been thoroughly heated, one should cast into it a gold ring weighing five *raktikas*, or one made of silver and so forth, which has been washed once. Then, having performed the rites beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the oblation (*havana*), as prescribed for the balance ordeal, together with the ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Oṃ,
you are the supreme purifier, the nectar of clarified butter, in sacrificial rites.
"O purifier, become even more purifying; O cold as snow, become hot! (301) [Pi 178].

With this, he should consecrate [the water]. Then the judge, having observed a fast and being dressed in wet clothes after bathing, shall place the written confession upon the head of the person to be purified.
Om.
"O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, speak the truth regarding my merits and sins.

(302) [Yājñavalkyasmṛti 2.104] Having consecrated [the ghee] with this mantra, one should lift the ring from the ghee—using the thumb and index finger—from the sound produced by the suction made upon placing a fresh leaf. Or, one should lift a heated bean from a mixture of ghee and oil. If it remains unburnt, then he is pure.
Now follows the rule regarding the fruit [of the ordeal].
Bṛhaspati says: "An iron ploughshare weighing twelve palas is called a *phāla*."
It should be eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide.
Then, while it is glowing like fire, the thief should lick it once with his tongue.
If he is not burned, he shall attain purification; otherwise, he is defeated.
"The thief here is a thief of cattle;

to the thief of cattle, the punishment of licking a heated iron plowshare must be given"—according to this *smṛti* text, so say the Maithilas. In this case as well, it follows immediately after the mantra beginning with "Thou, O Agni... (RV 10.87.2).
"One should also prescribe it for one who licks an iron [image] with the tongue.
(Dhko 523) Thus, as stated by Pitāmaha, the consecration of the fire (*agnyabhimantraṇa*) must be performed by both the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) and the person undergoing the ordeal.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

One should heat in the fire a plowshare (*phāla*) made of iron, weighing forty *tolakas*, measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length with eight barley-corns (*yava*) at its center, and likewise four finger-breadths in width. Therein, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*), having performed the rites beginning with the invocation of Dharma (*dharmāvāhana*) and ending with the oblation (*havana*), and having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), [should recite]:
O Agni, you are the four Vedas, and you are the one invoked in sacrifices;
you are the mouth of all the gods, and you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman.
Since you abide within the bellies of all living beings, you therefore know both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Because you indeed purify (pāvayasi) evil, therefore you are called Pāvaka.
O Pāvaka, reveal yourself among the wicked and be full of flames;
or else, through your pure nature, O Consumer of Oblations, become cool.
You alone move within all beings like a witness;
O God, you alone know those things which humans do not perceive. This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification.
"Therefore, you ought to protect him from this doubt in accordance with Dharma.
With these words, one should consecrate the fire situated in the vessel.
But the one to be purified shall say: "O Agni, Purifier, you who move within all beings like a witness over merits and sins, O Sage, speak the truth for me. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.104]
Having consecrated with this [mantra], he should lick the plowshare, which has the color of fire, once with his tongue. If he is not burned, he is purified.
Now follows the procedure for the *dharmaja* [trial]. Bṛhaspati says:
On two leaves, one should write "Dharma" and "Adharma," white and black respectively,
while reciting mantras such as those for the gift of life, the Gāyatrī and other Sāman chants, and so forth. Having addressed them, one should worship them with white and black perfumes and flowers.
Then, having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and enclosed them within lumps of clay,
one should make them equal and place them in a new jar, remaining unobserved.
Then, one should take a single lump from the jar without delay.
When the Dharma is grasped, one becomes pure and worthy of worship by the examiners. (315) As for the mantra for the gift of life, it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
"The power of the joined *pāśa* and *aṅkuśa*, adorned with the *vāṇī* and the *bindu*."
The seven [syllables] beginning with *yā* and ending with *sa*, followed by *vyoma* (ha) conjoined with the moon of truth (the bindu), form the first part.

At the end of that should be the *haṃsa*-mantra; then one should utter the word *amuṣya* (of such-and-such), and after that, one should say *prāṇāḥ* (vital breaths), and following that, *iha prāṇāḥ* (vital breaths here). 316–317. [Śāti 23.72–73]
One should say, "The life-force of such-and-such a person, staying here, has gone from there to the place of such-and-such.
At the end of "all the sense-faculties" (*sarvendriyāṇi*), one should finally add "speech, mind, and sight.
At the words "ear and nose," one should say, "the vital breaths have come here and shall remain in happiness for a long time."
Let this Prāṇamantra, which is proclaimed here at the end as the "bride of fire," stand aside for now.
One should employ the elements beginning with the noose (pāśa) prior to each word of the target name;
this is declared by the wise to be the Prāṇamantra in ritual applications.

By the phrase "the power [consisting of] the noose, goad, and folded hands," first is the seed-syllable of the noose, *oṃ*; then the seed-syllable of power, *hrīṃ*; then the seed-syllable of the goad, *kroṃ*. Thus: *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ*. The letter *ya* adorned with a bindu becomes *yaṃ*. Taking the seven letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa*, having extracted the letter *ya* [from each], there are the seven goads (*aṅkuśa*), wind (*vāyu*), fire (*anala*), fire (*agni*), and water (*varuṇa*) seed-syllables. (320)

Because it has been stated thus, the separate presentation of the seven [syllables] is for the purpose of showing that they possess the nasal drop (*bindu*). For this very reason, they are called "seeds" (*bīja*) elsewhere. "Adorned by Vyoman, Satya, and Indu": *Vyoman* is the syllable *ha*, *Satya* is the syllable *u*, and *Indu* is the *bindu*. Thus, *ahoṃ* is an illustration for the name of the deity in the genitive case, as in "of such-and-such. For it is said: "Whatever form appears in a mantra in place of the word 'that' (*adaḥ*), one should employ that form in that position as the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). (321)

Thus it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya. "Agnivadhūḥ svāhā. However, if there is no knowledge of the *gāyatrī* and other *sāmans*, one should recite only the *gāyatrī* together with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*.

"Whatever [rites] such as *japa* and *homa* have been prescribed in their entirety, if they cannot be performed, one should perform them all with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī*, and the *praṇava*. (Yogayājñavalkya-tantra 3.325)
Thus, from the observation of the statement in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* cited in the *Mitākṣarā*,
it is likewise inferred here regarding Pitāmaha:
"Now I shall fully explain the examination of dharma and adharma."
For men who have committed murder, who are entreating for mercy, and who seek expiation,
one should cause a representation of Dharma and Adharma to be made of silver, with their respective forms.
One should write Dharma and Adharma, white and black respectively, upon birch bark or a cloth.
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
White flowers represent Dharma, while black flowers represent Adharma.
Having prepared this and drawn the design, one should place those two [offerings] within the two ritual balls (piṇḍa).
Then, two equal-sized lumps should be made, either from cow dung or from clay.
They should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel,
unobserved, in a clean, smeared place in the presence of the deity and the Brahmins.
Then one should invoke the gods and the world-protectors as before;
having first performed the invocation of Dharma, one should write the document of oath:
"If I am free from sin, may Dharma come to my hand. [Pi 186–187ab]
The accused should, without delay, choose one of the two;
if he chooses the *dharma*, he shall be purified, but if he chooses the *adharma*, he shall lose his case.

Thus has the examination of dharma and adharma been briefly explained. (330) [Pi 189] "Of those who strike" refers to cases of violent assault; "of those who beg" refers to cases of extreme demands for wealth; "of those seeking expiation" refers to cases involving sin.
In this regard, the application is as follows:

Having placed upon two leaves the figures of Dharma and Adharma—one white and one black—in the form of dolls, one should perform the rite of infusing life (*jīvadāna*) into the image of Dharma with the mantra: *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ hoṃ haṃsaḥ; the vital breaths of Dharma are here, the vital breaths are here; the soul of Dharma is stationed here; speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths of Dharma, having come here, may you remain happily for a long time, svāhā!* Having performed this for the image of Adharma in the same manner, if there is knowledge of the *Gāyatrī* and other Sāman chants, one should use them; otherwise, having recited the *Gāyatrī* together with the *Praṇava* and the *Vyāhṛtis*, and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for Dharma, one should fashion Dharma from a lump of clay mixed with white flowers and Adharma from a lump mixed with black flowers, and place them in a new pitcher. Then the judge, in the presence of the gods and Brahmins, having performed the rites from the invocation of Dharma up to the oblation (*havana*), and having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), shall write the document of the oath (*pratijñāpatra*) accompanied by mantras and place it upon the head of the person to be purified (*śodhya*). As for the person to be purified:
"Oṃ!
If I am free from sin, may Dharma come into my hand!
(331) Having uttered this, one should take one of the two [substances] from the jar. If Dharma is taken, he is pure; otherwise, he is impure.
Now follows the procedure for oaths. Manu says:
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons.
A Vaiśya by means of a cow, seed, and gold; a Śūdra by all the mortal sins (pātaka).

(332) [M 8.113] Or he should cause him to touch separately the heads of his son and wife. (333) [M 8.114cd] He should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by making him utter: "This was done by me, or it was not done," and by the pronouncement of truth. One should cause the falsehood or deception that might be suspected to be established as the falsehood or untruth of what he has said. The meaning is that one should make him understand: "What I have spoken is the truth."

Kātyāyana states the manner of determining that: "He for whom no terrible calamity—whether caused by the king or by fate—occurs until the fourteenth day, is to be known as pure in his oath. (334) [K 463]

*Vyasana* means calamity; *ghora* means causing extreme affliction. Because it is a property of the body, it refers to the aforementioned diseases and so forth. Thus, for a Kṣatriya who utters a declaration such as "Was this done by me, or was it not? one should touch him with a vehicle, and likewise with a weapon. For a Vaiśya, one should do so with any one of these: a cow, seed-grain, or gold. Regarding the phrase "with all sins," this is because they are causes of sin through their improper use. By "all sins" is meant the aforementioned cow, grain, and gold taken together. Therefore, for a Śūdra who utters a declaration such as "Was this done by me, or was it not? one should touch him with all three: the cow, the grain, and the gold. If one asks what the authority is for touching these, [the answer follows].

"Or he should touch the heads of his son or his wife separately"—because such is seen in another statement of Manu; "enaṃ" refers to this person performing the oath. Therefore, while uttering the declaration, "Has this been done by me or not? he should touch the head of either his son or his wife. The same should be understood for the touching to be described below. Furthermore, the touching is to be performed with the right hand, since when an action is prescribed but the body part of the agent is not specified, [the right hand is to be used].

"In this context, the right hand should be understood as that which has reached the further shore of ritual actions," according to the statement of Kātyāyana. For this very reason, Viṣṇu has prescribed the use of dūrvā grass and other items in the hand,
as follows:
In all matters involving property, one should establish gold as the standard of value.
In that regard, for a debt of one *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a *śūdra* to swear an oath by holding *dūrvā* grass;
for a debt of two *kṛṣṇalas*, one should cause him to swear by holding sesame seeds.
For a debt of three *kṛṣṇalas*, he shall pay a handfull of water;
for four *kṛṣṇalas*, a *suvarṇa*;
for five *kṛṣṇalas*, land recovered from the furrow.
A treasury fine of less than half a *suvarṇa* shall be imposed on a *śūdra*.
Likewise: [Vi 9.10] Thus it is said.
When the value of the object is double, the agreement for a Vaiśya shall be as prescribed;
[344] when the value is triple, for a Rājanya;
[345] and when the value is quadruple, for a Brāhmaṇa. [346]
Thus [it is said]. "Less than a *kṛṣṇala*" means less than the value of a *rattikā* of gold.
Likewise, Bṛhaspati states elsewhere:
"Truth, vehicles, weapons, cows, seeds, and gold..."
"The feet of gods and Brahmins, and the heads of one's sons and wife—
these oaths have been declared as always easy to perform in matters of small value.
In cases of violent crimes (sāhasa) and formal accusations, they say that divine ordeals (divya) are the means of purification."

"In a very small matter" means that its scope is limited compared to the objects of oaths such as those concerning *dharma* (virtue) and so forth. Here, because oaths are presented as distinct from *divya* (ordeals), and because they are not enumerated among the *ghaṭa* (balance) and other ordeals, they do not possess the nature of an ordeal (*divyatva*). Consequently, there is no extension (*atideśa*) here of the rules for ordeals—such as fasting or wearing wet clothes—and so forth. However, for the sake of purity, one must observe care regarding bathing, sipping water (*ācamana*), and other such rites.
Yama says: "But having made a false oath involving the killing of an insect..."
A man is joined with falsehood and likewise with slaughter;
therefore, a man should not take an oath that involves a false desire for killing.

The term "of an insect" (*kīṭasya*) is an illustration intended to include all living beings. Therefore, the meaning is that an oath joined with the killing of even a creature of no utility whatsoever is a cause of misfortune; thus, the one who makes a false oath is joined with the sin of that killing.
Thus ends the *Divyatattva* (The Doctrine of Ordeals) within the *Smṛtitattva* composed by Śrī Raghunandana Bhaṭṭācārya, son of Śrī Haridhara Bhaṭṭācārya, of the Vadhyaghaṭī family.
